summary: This note explains peak ground acceleration (PGA), the maximum ground acceleration recorded at a site during an earthquake, and how it is measured, split into horizontal and vertical components, and used in seismic engineering and hazard mapping. It contrasts PGA, an instrumental measure of how much the ground shakes at a point, with magnitude scales and the felt-based Mercalli intensity scale. It also includes a USGS instrumental intensity table correlating acceleration and velocity with perceived shaking and damage, and a table of notable earthquakes with their maximum recorded PGA values.
one_line: Peak ground acceleration (PGA) is the maximum ground acceleration recorded at a site during an earthquake, used in engineering and seismic hazard mapping.
key_facts: PGA is equal to the amplitude of the largest absolute acceleration recorded on an accelerogram at a site during a particular earthquake.
Unlike the Richter and moment magnitude scales, PGA is not a measure of the total energy of an earthquake but of how much the earth shakes at a given geographic point.
The peak horizontal acceleration (PHA) is the most commonly used type of ground acceleration in engineering applications.
For moderate earthquakes, PGA is a reasonably good determinant of damage; in severe earthquakes, damage is more often correlated with peak ground velocity.
Shallow-focused earthquakes generate stronger shaking (acceleration) than intermediate and deep quakes, since the energy is released closer to the surface.
1 g = 9.81 m/s, and 1 Gal is equal to 0.01 m/s (1 g = 981 Gal).
In seismic engineering, the effective peak acceleration (EPA) tends to be ⅔ – ¾ the PGA.
Generally, 0.001 g is perceptible by people, 0.02 g causes people to lose their balance, and 0.50 g is very high, where well-designed buildings can survive if the duration is short.
The United States Geological Survey developed an Instrumental Intensity scale that maps peak ground acceleration and peak ground velocity on an intensity scale similar to the felt Mercalli scale.
In the 7-class Japan Meteorological Agency seismic intensity scale, the highest intensity, Shindo 7, covers accelerations greater than 4 m/s (0.41 g).
In India, areas with expected PGA values higher than 0.36 g are classed as "Zone 5", or "Very High Damage Risk Zone".
The highest recorded single-direction PGA in the note is 4.36 g, from the 2008 Iwate–Miyagi Nairiku earthquake (magnitude 6.9, depth 8 km, 12 fatalities).
The 2016 Kaikōura earthquake (magnitude 7.8, depth 15 km) recorded a single-direction PGA of 3.23 g, with 2 fatalities.
The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami (magnitude 9.1, depth 30 km, 19,759 fatalities) recorded a single-direction PGA of 2.7 g and a vector-sum PGA of 2.99 g.
The 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquake (magnitude 7.8, depth 10 km) had 57,658 fatalities and a recorded PGA of 1.62 g.
